messages.body_plain:
the fitted values are often, but not always, what is used to predict
missing data, like the 'mean' and the associated 'stdev'. its all about
having information about the linear predictor and try to use that to
predict a missing datapoint. you can do that from the linear.predictor
or fitted.values ouput, or by using posterior.sample().

the sampling should work, if it does not, make sure try with R-4.1 and a
new testing version. if memory is a concern, then try adding

	inla(..., inla.mode="experimental")

> > > > > > > Hi,

> > > > > > > you may have already considered this, but I have to ask
> > > > > > > since it's such a common conceptual mistake:
> > > > > > > The linear predictor output (and link-funcion transformed
> > > > > > > version in fitted.values) give the credible intervals for
> > > > > > > the linear predictor for "known" observations, and
> > > > > > > prediction intervals for the linear predictor for the
> > > > > > > "missing" observations (they are both prediction intervals
> > > > > > > for the linear predictor), and _not_ for the observation
> > > > > > > model itself. For that, you need to take the observation
> > > > > > > distribution into account as well.  The easiest general
> > > > > > > way to do that is to generate samples of the predictor
> > > > > > > with inla.posterior.sample, and then sample the
> > > > > > > observation model conditionally on that.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > In other words, if m is the observation expectation
> > > > > > > conditionally on the latent variables (i.e. the
> > > > > > > predictor), the
> > > > > > >   E(Y|data) = E(E(Y|m,data)) = E(m|data)
> > > > > > > and
> > > > > > >   Var(Y|data) = E(Var(Y|m,data)) + Var(E(Y|m,data)) =
> > > > > > > E(Var(Y|m,data)) + Var(m|data)
> > > > > > > The fitted.values output gives you E(m|data) and
> > > > > > > Var(m|data), but not E(Var(Y|m,data)).
> > > > > > > That last term can sometimes be obtained from the
> > > > > > > hyperparameter summary, but if you want more accurate
> > > > > > > prediction intervals for Y you need more (that you can get
> > > > > > > via sampling).
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Finn

messages.subject: inla.spde2.matern
messages.body_plain:
Hi

I would like to translate a geospatial model to inla with the appropriate prior distributions. This mostly works as desired, but I do not know how to set my priors properly for the spatial field. I assume a exponential correlation of the form
cor(s1, s2) = sigma^2 * exp(- rho * dist(s1, s2))
and I would like to set priors 1/sigma^2 ~ Gamma(a1, a2) and rho ~ Unif(b1,b2). Is this possible with INLA?
I have read Lindgren and Rue and several books but can not find a solution which comes close. So far I use
inla.spde2.matern(mesh, alpha = 1.5) or
inla.spde2.pcmatern(mesh, alpha = 1.5, prior.range = c(0.3, 0.5), prior.sigma = c(10, 0.01))
For the inla.spde2.matern there are options prior.variance.nomial, prior.range.nominal which sound promising. However I could not find a documentation as to what they do exactly which I could understand.

Any help is appreciated, thanks in advanced.
messages.body_snippet:
Hi

I would like to translate a geospatial model to inla with the appropriate prior distributions. This mostly works as desired, but I do not know how to set my priors properly for the spatial field.

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] inla.spde2.matern
messages.body_plain:
Hi Dan,

the sigma-prior is possible; I'm not sure if the "uniform on a finite interval" prior for rho is possible.

The inla.spde2.matern implements a general family that links a set of theta-parameters to tau and kappa in an spde formulation of the Matern family, (kappa^2-Laplacian)^(alpha/2)(tau x(s)) = W(s) (see the function help text).
The parameter link is user-defined, so allows some flexibility.
Smoothness:
  nu = alpha - dim/2 = 0.5 for alpha=1.5.
Variance:
  sigma^2 = const / kappa^(2*nu) / tau^2
Precision:
  1/sigma^2 = kappa * tau^2 / const
The range controlling parameter rho in your parameterisation is kappa (i.e. rho is proportional to the inverse range), so
  theta1 = log(1/sigma^2) = - log(const) + log(kappa) + 2*log(tau)
  theta2 = log(rho) = log(kappa)
Solving for log(tau) and log(kappa),
  log(tau) = -log(const) / 2 + theta1 / 2 + theta2
  log(kappa) = theta2,
so you need
  B.tau = cbind(-log(const) / 2, 1/2, 1)
  B.kappa = cbind(0, 0, 1)
in order to get theta1 and theta2 to be the log() of 1/sigma^2 and rho.
The constant "const" can be derived from the expression for the variance in Lindgren et al (2011, JRSSB) or Lindgren and Rue 2015 (https://www.jstatsoft.org/article/view/v063i19).

You can then set the prior for theta1 to a loggamma(a1,a2) distribution to get your desired prior for 1/sigma^2, via
  hyper=list(theta1=list(...))

For theta2, you'd be looking for a prior with density  exp(theta2)/(b2-b1) on the interval (log(b1), log(b2)),
which isn't directly available. I see there's an "expression" prior model that might be able to specify a general density expression, but the finite interval support is bound to cause problems.

So in summary, yes, it's partly possible, but in particular the rho-prior is a bit problematic, and from a modelling perspective it's probably better to use the pc-prior option via inla.spde2.pcmatern instead.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Hi Håvard and team.

In Section 1.3 in the INLA paper <https://rss.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1467-9868.2008.00700.x> the authors define a LGM. They write the density of the latent field x conditional to a hyperparameter vector Theta1, and the density of y conditional to a hyperparameter vector Theta2. Later they join Theta1 and Theta2 into one unique hyperparameter vector Theta.

I'm new to the topic and I'm not sure I understand correctly the logic behind this formulation. Could you give an example of a hyperparameter that could go into Theta2?

Thank you

Guillermina

finn.l...@gmail.com schrieb am Donnerstag, 16. September 2021 um 18:37:51 UTC+2:
> Hi,
>
> yes, you're right, I missed one of the 1/2 factors, as well as the sign on the log(const).
>
> And yes, the hyper argument is for the f() specification, as you wrote in your other reply.
> (Or you can alter the spde object by replacing the contents of spde$f$hyper.default instead, after the inla.spde2.matern call and before setting up the inla model.)
>
> Finn
>
> On Thu, 16 Sept 2021 at 13:54, dan <twitter.is...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Hi Finn
> >
> > Thank you very much for this quick and thorough response, that helps me a lot. Just to clarify details in you calculation:
> >
> >   theta1 = log(1/sigma^2) = - log(const) + log(kappa) + 2*log(tau)
> >   theta2 = log(rho) = log(kappa)
> > Solving for log(tau) and log(kappa),
> >   log(tau) = -log(const) / 2 + theta1 / 2 + theta2
> >   log(kappa) = theta2,
> > so you need
> >   B.tau = cbind(-log(const) / 2, 1/2, 1)
> >   B.kappa = cbind(0, 0, 1)
> >
> > I got:
> > Solving for log(tau) and log(kappa),
> >   log(tau) = + log(const) / 2 + theta1 / 2 - theta2 /2
> >   log(kappa) = theta2,
> > so you need
> >   B.tau = cbind(+ log(const) / 2, 1/2,  - 1/2)
> >   B.kappa = cbind(0, 0, 1)
> >
> > Do you agree?
> >
> > Assuming that I would like a Gamma prior also for the kappa (alias rho), the call to inla.spde2.matern is then
> > INLA::inla.spde2.matern(
> >   mesh = mesh,
> >   alpha = 1.5,
> >   B.tau = cbind(log(const) / 2, .5, -.5),
> >   B.kappa = cbind(0, 0, 1),
> >   hyper = list(theta1 = list(param = c(a1, a2), prior = "loggamma"),
> >                theta2 = list(param = c(b1, b2), prior = "loggamma"))
> > )?
> > I just ask because there is no hyper argument specified for the inla.spde2.matern and I have learned not to trust the ... argument too much in R.
> > I have to wrap my head around how to get a suitable value for this const and will consider the resources that you have suggested, thanks again.
> >
> > Dan
> >
> >
> > finn.l...@gmail.com schrieb am Donnerstag, 16. September 2021 um 12:20:55 UTC+2:
> > > Hi Dan,
> > >
> > > the sigma-prior is possible; I'm not sure if the "uniform on a finite interval" prior for rho is possible.
> > >
> > > The inla.spde2.matern implements a general family that links a set of theta-parameters to tau and kappa in an spde formulation of the Matern family, (kappa^2-Laplacian)^(alpha/2)(tau x(s)) = W(s) (see the function help text).
> > > The parameter link is user-defined, so allows some flexibility.
> > > Smoothness:
> > >   nu = alpha - dim/2 = 0.5 for alpha=1.5.
> > > Variance:
> > >   sigma^2 = const / kappa^(2*nu) / tau^2
> > > Precision:
> > >   1/sigma^2 = kappa * tau^2 / const
> > > The range controlling parameter rho in your parameterisation is kappa (i.e. rho is proportional to the inverse range), so
> > >   theta1 = log(1/sigma^2) = - log(const) + log(kappa) + 2*log(tau)
> > >   theta2 = log(rho) = log(kappa)
> > > Solving for log(tau) and log(kappa),
> > >   log(tau) = -log(const) / 2 + theta1 / 2 + theta2
> > >   log(kappa) = theta2,
> > > so you need
> > >   B.tau = cbind(-log(const) / 2, 1/2, 1)
> > >   B.kappa = cbind(0, 0, 1)
> > > in order to get theta1 and theta2 to be the log() of 1/sigma^2 and rho.
> > > The constant "const" can be derived from the expression for the variance in Lindgren et al (2011, JRSSB) or Lindgren and Rue 2015 (https://www.jstatsoft.org/article/view/v063i19).
> > >
> > > You can then set the prior for theta1 to a loggamma(a1,a2) distribution to get your desired prior for 1/sigma^2, via
> > >   hyper=list(theta1=list(...))
> > >
> > > For theta2, you'd be looking for a prior with density  exp(theta2)/(b2-b1) on the interval (log(b1), log(b2)),
> > > which isn't directly available. I see there's an "expression" prior model that might be able to specify a general density expression, but the finite interval support is bound to cause problems.
> > >
> > > So in summary, yes, it's partly possible, but in particular the rho-prior is a bit problematic, and from a modelling perspective it's probably better to use the pc-prior option via inla.spde2.pcmatern instead.
> > >
> > > Finn
> > >
> > > On Thu, 16 Sept 2021 at 10:48, dan <twitter.is...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > Hi
> > > >
> > > > I would like to translate a geospatial model to inla with the appropriate prior distributions. This mostly works as desired, but I do not know how to set my priors properly for the spatial field. I assume a exponential correlation of the form
> > > > cor(s1, s2) = sigma^2 * exp(- rho * dist(s1, s2))
> > > > and I would like to set priors 1/sigma^2 ~ Gamma(a1, a2) and rho ~ Unif(b1,b2). Is this possible with INLA?
> > > > I have read Lindgren and Rue and several books but can not find a solution which comes close. So far I use
> > > > inla.spde2.matern(mesh, alpha = 1.5) or
> > > > inla.spde2.pcmatern(mesh, alpha = 1.5, prior.range = c(0.3, 0.5), prior.sigma = c(10, 0.01))
> > > > For the inla.spde2.matern there are options prior.variance.nomial, prior.range.nominal which sound promising. However I could not find a documentation as to what they do exactly which I could understand.
> > > >
> > > > Any help is appreciated, thanks in advanced.
> > > >
> > > > --

Hi Håvard,

Thanks so much for your help and such a helpful answer!

Using the "...scale=1/w" variable does indeed result in very similar results being obtained by INLA and MCMCglmm. I'd imagine the slight differences are likely due to variation in priors and the INLA vs full MCMC methods. I'll be sure to check my correct implementation of this method further.

Thanks again,
Will

messages.body_snippet:
Hi Finn,

As a very simple example, the code would be something like m=inla(formula=y~x1+ns(x2, df=n), data=dat). The inlabru syntax doesn’t seem to allow you to use a function like ns() in this case.

messages.body_plain:
I wasn’t actually aware of this working in inla either; I assume that the ns() function returns a matrix that then gets used as a fixed matrix?
If that’s the case, there will be ways of specifying such models in inlabru, e.g. by calling ns directly in the predictor expression and multiplying it with a vector of latent coefficients.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Ok, that makes sense.

Currently, inlabru only supports matrix covariate input in the predictor expressions and not in the component definitions themselves, but I was thinking of how to add support for it just this week; when that’s done it will likely work like this:
 compname(ns(x1,df=n)),
just as for regular vector covariates. For precomputed named matrices, e.g. data=list(X=ns(x1,df=n)), the component definition ~ X would then also work, since those are converted to the more explicit ~ X(X, model=“linear”)
The main caveat is that I’m not sure if that equivalence actually holds in the inla f() definitions or not; I’ll discover that in testing, and solve it differently if needed; it’s a straightforward model, so it’s just the internal implementation details that may be different than expected.

Finn

>  compname(ns(x1,df=n)),

Currently, you can do something like

messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

Does anyone know if it is possible to fit a "logistic Gaussian process regression model" with INLA?

The model can be found in the below link:

It's simply works by replacing linear predictors with a GP to make Logistic regression non-linear. It's computationally hard to fit it using MCMC so I am wondering if it's possible to fit it using INLA. Any help would be appreciated.

messages.subject: Phylogenetic modelling in inla and brms
messages.subject_clean: Phylogenetic modelling in inla and brms
messages.body_plain:
I am in the process of switching from brms to inla for some simple phylogenteic analyses, but in simulations, I am seeing some differences between my inla and brms results, primarily, the amount of variation captured by the phylogeny relative to residual variation. For example

set.seed(1)
library(ape)
library(Rphylopars)
library(phytools)
library(INLA)
library(brms)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

cmb_df = NULL
for(a in 1:10){
  print(a)
  sim_data = simtraits(ntaxa = 20,ntraits = 1,nreps = 1,nmissing = 0)
  traits = sim_data$trait_data
  phy_sig = phylosig(sim_data$tree, traits$V1, method = "lambda")

  sp_mat_inla = vcv(sim_data$tree, corr = F)
  #Code for making precision matrix copied from https://royalsocietypublishing.org/doi/10.1098/rspb.2019.2817
  sp_mat_inla <- sp_mat_inla / exp(determinant(sp_mat_inla)$modulus[1] /
                                     nrow(sp_mat_inla))
  prec_mat <- solve(sp_mat_inla)
  prec_mat = inla.as.sparse(prec_mat)

  traits = traits %>%
    left_join(tibble(species = rownames(sp_mat_inla),
                     phy_id = 1:nrow(sp_mat_inla)))

  m_inla <- inla(V1 ~
                   f(phy_id, model = "generic0", Cmatrix = prec_mat, constr = T),
                 data = traits, family = "gaussian")
  sd_inla = summary(m_inla)

  phy_inla = (sd_inla$hyperpar[2,1]^-1)/(sd_inla$hyperpar[1,1]^-1 + sd_inla$hyperpar[2,1]^-1) #Variance captured by the phylogeny relative to the residual error variance

  sp_mat_brm = vcv(sim_data$tree, corr = T)
  m_brm = brm(V1 ~
                (1| gr(species, cov = sp_mat_brm)),
              data = traits, data2 = list(sp_mat_brm = sp_mat_brm),
              chains = 2, cores = 2)
  sm_brm = summary(m_brm)
  phy_brm = (sm_brm$random[[1]][1,1]^2)/(sm_brm$spec_pars[1,1]^2 + sm_brm$random[[1]][1,1]^2) #Variance captured by the phylogeny relative to the residual error variance

  df = data.frame(
    run = a,
    phy_sig = phy_sig[[1]],
    phy_inla,
    phy_brm
  )
  cmb_df = rbind(cmb_df, df)
}

ggplot() +
  geom_point(data = cmb_df,
             aes(x = phy_brm, y = phy_inla)) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0.9, 1), ylim = c(0.9, 1))

If both inla and brms were producing the same model, I would expect these points to fall on a straight line where beta = 1

Am I missing something obvious in my inla code? Or is it an interpretation issue?

P.S. I have used default priors for both inla and brms.

Tom

messages.body_plain:
Hi THomas,

since the default priors are sure to be different in the different systems, that would be my first place to look...
Default priors really only exist to make coding faster in cases where the priors only have a minor influence, but in cases where the priors do matter, one needs to be more careful (and arguably, one needs to be careful also when the priors don't matter, since we usually don't know if they matter or not until we check!)

Finn

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Hello again

Unfortunately, the said solution does not work. I put together a reproducible example borrowed from https://becarioprecario.bitbucket.io/spde-gitbook/ch-intro.html :

rm(list = ls())
library(INLA)
pl.dom <- cbind(c(0, 1, 1, 0.7, 0), c(0, 0, 0.7, 1, 1))
mesh5 <- inla.mesh.2d(loc.domain = pl.dom, max.e = c(0.092, 0.2))
coords <- as.matrix(SPDEtoy[, 1:2])
A5 <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh5, loc = coords)
spde5 <- inla.spde2.matern(
  mesh = mesh5,
  alpha = 1.5,
  B.tau = matrix(c(-0.5 * log(4 * pi), 0.5,-0.5), 1, 3),
  B.kappa =  matrix(c(0, 0, 1), 1, 3)
)
stk5 <- inla.stack(
  data = list(resp = SPDEtoy$y),
  A = list(A5, 1),
  effects = list(i = 1:spde5$n.spde,
                 beta0 = rep(1, nrow(SPDEtoy))),
  tag = 'est'
)

# working default ---------------------------------------------------------
res5 <- inla(
  resp ~ 0 + beta0 + f(i, model = spde5),
  data = inla.stack.data(stk5),
  control.predictor = list(A = inla.stack.A(stk5))
)

# try1 to reset prior -----------------------------------------------------
res5 <- inla(
  resp ~ 0 + beta0 + f(
    i,
    model = spde5,
    hyper = list(
      theta1 = list(param = c(2.01, 1.01), prior = "loggamma"),
      theta2 = list(param = c(2.01, 1.01), prior = "loggamma")
    )
  ),
  data = inla.stack.data(stk5),
  control.predictor = list(A = inla.stack.A(stk5))
)

# try2 to reset prior -----------------------------------------------------
spde5$f$hyper.default <- list(
  theta1 = list(param = c(2.01, 1.01), prior = "loggamma"),
  theta2 = list(param = c(2.01, 1.01), prior = "loggamma")
)
res5 <- inla(
  resp ~ 0 + beta0 + f(i, model = spde5),
  data = inla.stack.data(stk5),
  control.predictor = list(A = inla.stack.A(stk5))
)

I get the following error:
Error in inla.set.hyper(model = model, section = "latent", hyper = hyper,  :
  Setting hyperparameter `theta2'. Key `prior' = 'none' is 'read-only', cannot change to `loggamma'.

I could not find the inla.set.hyper in the documentation for the users, so I can not tell what is wrong, but telling from the 'read-only' hint, is it forbidden to change priors for theta1 and theta2? Is there a way to work around this, or have I misunderstood some of the hints above?

Best, Dan

dan schrieb am Freitag, 17. September 2021 um 12:56:10 UTC+2:
> Great! Thanks for the clarifications.
>
> finn.l...@gmail.com schrieb am Donnerstag, 16. September 2021 um 18:37:51 UTC+2:
> > Hi,
> >
> > yes, you're right, I missed one of the 1/2 factors, as well as the sign on the log(const).
> >
> > And yes, the hyper argument is for the f() specification, as you wrote in your other reply.
> > (Or you can alter the spde object by replacing the contents of spde$f$hyper.default instead, after the inla.spde2.matern call and before setting up the inla model.)
> >
> > Finn
> >
> > On Thu, 16 Sept 2021 at 13:54, dan <twitter.is...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > Hi Finn
> > >
> > > Thank you very much for this quick and thorough response, that helps me a lot. Just to clarify details in you calculation:
> > >
> > >   theta1 = log(1/sigma^2) = - log(const) + log(kappa) + 2*log(tau)
> > >   theta2 = log(rho) = log(kappa)
> > > Solving for log(tau) and log(kappa),
> > >   log(tau) = -log(const) / 2 + theta1 / 2 + theta2
> > >   log(kappa) = theta2,
> > > so you need
> > >   B.tau = cbind(-log(const) / 2, 1/2, 1)
> > >   B.kappa = cbind(0, 0, 1)
> > >
> > > I got:
> > > Solving for log(tau) and log(kappa),
> > >   log(tau) = + log(const) / 2 + theta1 / 2 - theta2 /2
> > >   log(kappa) = theta2,
> > > so you need
> > >   B.tau = cbind(+ log(const) / 2, 1/2,  - 1/2)
> > >   B.kappa = cbind(0, 0, 1)
> > >
> > > Do you agree?
> > >
> > > Assuming that I would like a Gamma prior also for the kappa (alias rho), the call to inla.spde2.matern is then
> > > INLA::inla.spde2.matern(
> > >   mesh = mesh,
> > >   alpha = 1.5,
> > >   B.tau = cbind(log(const) / 2, .5, -.5),
> > >   B.kappa = cbind(0, 0, 1),
> > >   hyper = list(theta1 = list(param = c(a1, a2), prior = "loggamma"),
> > >                theta2 = list(param = c(b1, b2), prior = "loggamma"))
> > > )?
> > > I just ask because there is no hyper argument specified for the inla.spde2.matern and I have learned not to trust the ... argument too much in R.
> > > I have to wrap my head around how to get a suitable value for this const and will consider the resources that you have suggested, thanks again.
> > >
> > > Dan
> > >
> > >
> > > finn.l...@gmail.com schrieb am Donnerstag, 16. September 2021 um 12:20:55 UTC+2:
> > > > Hi Dan,
> > > >
> > > > the sigma-prior is possible; I'm not sure if the "uniform on a finite interval" prior for rho is possible.
> > > >
> > > > The inla.spde2.matern implements a general family that links a set of theta-parameters to tau and kappa in an spde formulation of the Matern family, (kappa^2-Laplacian)^(alpha/2)(tau x(s)) = W(s) (see the function help text).
> > > > The parameter link is user-defined, so allows some flexibility.
> > > > Smoothness:
> > > >   nu = alpha - dim/2 = 0.5 for alpha=1.5.
> > > > Variance:
> > > >   sigma^2 = const / kappa^(2*nu) / tau^2
> > > > Precision:
> > > >   1/sigma^2 = kappa * tau^2 / const
> > > > The range controlling parameter rho in your parameterisation is kappa (i.e. rho is proportional to the inverse range), so
> > > >   theta1 = log(1/sigma^2) = - log(const) + log(kappa) + 2*log(tau)
> > > >   theta2 = log(rho) = log(kappa)
> > > > Solving for log(tau) and log(kappa),
> > > >   log(tau) = -log(const) / 2 + theta1 / 2 + theta2
> > > >   log(kappa) = theta2,
> > > > so you need
> > > >   B.tau = cbind(-log(const) / 2, 1/2, 1)
> > > >   B.kappa = cbind(0, 0, 1)
> > > > in order to get theta1 and theta2 to be the log() of 1/sigma^2 and rho.
> > > > The constant "const" can be derived from the expression for the variance in Lindgren et al (2011, JRSSB) or Lindgren and Rue 2015 (https://www.jstatsoft.org/article/view/v063i19).
> > > >
> > > > You can then set the prior for theta1 to a loggamma(a1,a2) distribution to get your desired prior for 1/sigma^2, via
> > > >   hyper=list(theta1=list(...))
> > > >
> > > > For theta2, you'd be looking for a prior with density  exp(theta2)/(b2-b1) on the interval (log(b1), log(b2)),
> > > > which isn't directly available. I see there's an "expression" prior model that might be able to specify a general density expression, but the finite interval support is bound to cause problems.
> > > >
> > > > So in summary, yes, it's partly possible, but in particular the rho-prior is a bit problematic, and from a modelling perspective it's probably better to use the pc-prior option via inla.spde2.pcmatern instead.
> > > >
> > > > Finn
> > > >
> > > > On Thu, 16 Sept 2021 at 10:48, dan <twitter.is...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > Hi
> > > > >
> > > > > I would like to translate a geospatial model to inla with the appropriate prior distributions. This mostly works as desired, but I do not know how to set my priors properly for the spatial field. I assume a exponential correlation of the form
> > > > > cor(s1, s2) = sigma^2 * exp(- rho * dist(s1, s2))
> > > > > and I would like to set priors 1/sigma^2 ~ Gamma(a1, a2) and rho ~ Unif(b1,b2). Is this possible with INLA?
> > > > > I have read Lindgren and Rue and several books but can not find a solution which comes close. So far I use
> > > > > inla.spde2.matern(mesh, alpha = 1.5) or
> > > > > inla.spde2.pcmatern(mesh, alpha = 1.5, prior.range = c(0.3, 0.5), prior.sigma = c(10, 0.01))
> > > > > For the inla.spde2.matern there are options prior.variance.nomial, prior.range.nominal which sound promising. However I could not find a documentation as to what they do exactly which I could understand.
> > > > >
> > > > > Any help is appreciated, thanks in advanced.

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Using inla.tmarginal with gaussian distribution and log link function
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Using inla.tmarginal with gaussian distribution and log link function
messages.body_plain:
the safe option is to always start from the marginal in the internal
scale, as those are more 'gaussian'-like, and transform from there. If
the problem is ''well behaved'' with enough data, then you can start
anywhere, but personally, I always convert from the internal scale.

to get the variance from the the log-precision, then do (as you suggest)

marg.variance = inla.tmarginal(
function(x) exp(-x),
mod$internal.marginals.hyperpar[[1]])

and then do summary

	inla.zmarginal(marg.variance)

personally, I like more stdev which is in an interpretable scale, then
use 'exp(-x/2)'

messages.subject: How to include SIR as as offset for forecasting period
messages.subject_clean: How to include SIR as as offset for forecasting period
messages.body_plain:
Hi INLA group members,

I am
working on a spatio-temporal model with type IV interaction to block level monthly
cases data from 502 small areas (block) covering a period from Jan 2013 to Dec
2020 (96 months) along environment and climate covariates. I have fitted the
model to the data covering Jan 2013 to Dec 2018 (training data set) and validated
the model to the data (test data set) to the period from Jan 2019-Dec 2020. For
your kind information while fitting and validating the model I have used the
standardized incidence rate (SIR) as an offset in R-INLA. SIR for each month
was calculated as a product of ‘r’ (ratio of total no. of cases to total
population in a year) and population in a month.

Now
I would like to apply the model to forecast the cases beyond the period of
observations (i.e. Jan 2021 to Dec 2021). Since, I do not have the case data
for the forecasting period, it would not be possible to calculate and include
the SIR as an offset for this period. In this respect I seek the advice of the
team on the following:

(i)
can I make predictions for the out of sample period (Jan 2021-Dec 2021) without
the offset?

(ii)
can I use the monthly case data or the mean no. of cases for the previous year
to calculate SIR (assuming the trend is same in 2021) and provide this as an offset.

(iii)
any other suggestions?

> > > > > )?

> > > > > > The parameter link is user-defined, so allows some flexibility.
> > > > > > Smoothness:
> > > > > >   nu = alpha - dim/2 = 0.5 for alpha=1.5.
> > > > > > Variance:
> > > > > >   sigma^2 = const / kappa^(2*nu) / tau^2
> > > > > > Precision:
> > > > > >   1/sigma^2 = kappa * tau^2 / const
> > > > > > The range controlling parameter rho in your parameterisation is kappa (i.e. rho is proportional to the inverse range), so
> > > > > >   theta1 = log(1/sigma^2) = - log(const) + log(kappa) + 2*log(tau)
> > > > > >   theta2 = log(rho) = log(kappa)
> > > > > > Solving for log(tau) and log(kappa),
> > > > > >   log(tau) = -log(const) / 2 + theta1 / 2 + theta2
> > > > > >   log(kappa) = theta2,
> > > > > > so you need
> > > > > >   B.tau = cbind(-log(const) / 2, 1/2, 1)

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] inla.spde2.matern
messages.body_plain:
Hi Dan,

I checked this with Haavard, and it turns out that the internals for the spde2 models can only use special multivariate priors; the default log-normal prior and the joint PC-prior for range and sigma are what's implemented.
Either one would need to add the gamma-product as a bivariate prior, or implement the model separately, via inla.rgeneric.

Since for ordinary modelling, I would recommend just using the PC-prior; there, sigma and 1/range are given Exponential priors (for dim=2; range^{-dim/2}~Exp for other dimensions).

Finn

Finn

> > > > > > On Thu, 16 Sept 2021 at 13:54, dan <twitter.is...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > > > Hi Finn
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Thank you very much for this quick and thorough response, that helps me a lot. Just to clarify details in you calculation:
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >   theta1 = log(1/sigma^2) = - log(const) + log(kappa) + 2*log(tau)
> > > > > > >   theta2 = log(rho) = log(kappa)

> > > > > > > so you need
> > > > > > >   B.tau = cbind(-log(const) / 2, 1/2, 1)
> > > > > > >   B.kappa = cbind(0, 0, 1)
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > I got:
> > > > > > > Solving for log(tau) and log(kappa),
> > > > > > >   log(tau) = + log(const) / 2 + theta1 / 2 - theta2 /2
> > > > > > >   log(kappa) = theta2,
> > > > > > > so you need
> > > > > > >   B.tau = cbind(+ log(const) / 2, 1/2,  - 1/2)

> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Do you agree?

> > > > > > > Assuming that I would like a Gamma prior also for the kappa (alias rho), the call to inla.spde2.matern is then
> > > > > > > INLA::inla.spde2.matern(
> > > > > > >   mesh = mesh,
> > > > > > >   alpha = 1.5,
> > > > > > >   B.tau = cbind(log(const) / 2, .5, -.5),
> > > > > > >   B.kappa = cbind(0, 0, 1),
> > > > > > >   hyper = list(theta1 = list(param = c(a1, a2), prior = "loggamma"),
> > > > > > >                theta2 = list(param = c(b1, b2), prior = "loggamma"))
> > > > > > > )?
> > > > > > > I just ask because there is no hyper argument specified for the inla.spde2.matern and I have learned not to trust the ... argument too much in R.
> > > > > > > I have to wrap my head around how to get a suitable value for this const and will consider the resources that you have suggested, thanks again.

> > > > > > > finn.l...@gmail.com schrieb am Donnerstag, 16. September 2021 um 12:20:55 UTC+2:
> > > > > > > > Hi Dan,
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > the sigma-prior is possible; I'm not sure if the "uniform on a finite interval" prior for rho is possible.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > The inla.spde2.matern implements a general family that links a set of theta-parameters to tau and kappa in an spde formulation of the Matern family, (kappa^2-Laplacian)^(alpha/2)(tau x(s)) = W(s) (see the function help text).
> > > > > > > > The parameter link is user-defined, so allows some flexibility.
> > > > > > > > Smoothness:
> > > > > > > >   nu = alpha - dim/2 = 0.5 for alpha=1.5.
> > > > > > > > Variance:
> > > > > > > >   sigma^2 = const / kappa^(2*nu) / tau^2
> > > > > > > > Precision:
> > > > > > > >   1/sigma^2 = kappa * tau^2 / const
> > > > > > > > The range controlling parameter rho in your parameterisation is kappa (i.e. rho is proportional to the inverse range), so
> > > > > > > >   theta1 = log(1/sigma^2) = - log(const) + log(kappa) + 2*log(tau)
> > > > > > > >   theta2 = log(rho) = log(kappa)
> > > > > > > > Solving for log(tau) and log(kappa),
> > > > > > > >   log(tau) = -log(const) / 2 + theta1 / 2 + theta2
> > > > > > > >   log(kappa) = theta2,
> > > > > > > > so you need
> > > > > > > >   B.tau = cbind(-log(const) / 2, 1/2, 1)
> > > > > > > >   B.kappa = cbind(0, 0, 1)
> > > > > > > > in order to get theta1 and theta2 to be the log() of 1/sigma^2 and rho.
> > > > > > > > The constant "const" can be derived from the expression for the variance in Lindgren et al (2011, JRSSB) or Lindgren and Rue 2015 (https://www.jstatsoft.org/article/view/v063i19).
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > You can then set the prior for theta1 to a loggamma(a1,a2) distribution to get your desired prior for 1/sigma^2, via
> > > > > > > >   hyper=list(theta1=list(...))
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > For theta2, you'd be looking for a prior with density  exp(theta2)/(b2-b1) on the interval (log(b1), log(b2)),
> > > > > > > > which isn't directly available. I see there's an "expression" prior model that might be able to specify a general density expression, but the finite interval support is bound to cause problems.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > So in summary, yes, it's partly possible, but in particular the rho-prior is a bit problematic, and from a modelling perspective it's probably better to use the pc-prior option via inla.spde2.pcmatern instead.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > Finn
> > > > > > > >

> > > > > > > > > and I would like to set priors 1/sigma^2 ~ Gamma(a1, a2) and rho ~ Unif(b1,b2). Is this possible with INLA?
> > > > > > > > > I have read Lindgren and Rue and several books but can not find a solution which comes close. So far I use
> > > > > > > > > inla.spde2.matern(mesh, alpha = 1.5) or
> > > > > > > > > inla.spde2.pcmatern(mesh, alpha = 1.5, prior.range = c(0.3, 0.5), prior.sigma = c(10, 0.01))
> > > > > > > > > For the inla.spde2.matern there are options prior.variance.nomial, prior.range.nominal which sound promising. However I could not find a documentation as to what they do exactly which I could understand.

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Data stack with more than one A matrix
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Data stack with more than one A matrix
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

for some reason the plain "Xbeta" use in the predictor doesn't work as intended, but one can access the latent vector directly, which does work.
One important consideration is also that it's generally unsafe to have completely automated know selections, since if one does that in the predictor expression, one gets different values for estimation and for prediction, so it's much safer to be explicit (can be data dependent, but needs to be controlled to ensure the same values are used in all the calculations).
See the following example. I'll look into why the direct latent vector access is needed, and also look into other ways of specifying these types of models; they're essentially the same as the 1d-mesh based spde models but with independent priors; those are handled automatically via the main_mapper, and one can make user-defined mapper objects, which could be used to define the "x-to-basis function" mapping for these splines, just as it's done for the B-splines in the 1D mesh models.

library(INLA)
library(inlabru)

# Random locations on (0, 20)
data <- data.frame(x1 = runif(100, min = 0, max = 20))
# A linear predictor plus noise
data$y <- data$x1 + rnorm(100)

fit <- bru(
  components = ~ -1 + Xbeta(1:4, model = "factor_full"),
  formula =
    y ~
    splines::ns(x1, knots = c(5, 10, 15), Boundary.knots = c(0, 20)) %*%
    Xbeta_latent,
  allow_latent = TRUE,
  data = data
)

summary(fit)
fit$summary.random$Xbeta

messages.body_plain:
Found the issue with the Xbeta vs beta_latent. The code below is an alternative that sets allow_combine=TRUE, which does allow the use of Xbeta.
But personally I think the version with direct use of Xbeta_latent is clearer.

library(INLA)
library(inlabru)

# Random locations on (0, 20)
data <- data.frame(x1 = runif(100, min = 0, max = 20))
# A linear predictor plus noise
data$y <- data$x1 + rnorm(100)

fit <- bru(
  components = ~ -1 + Xbeta(1:4, model = "factor_full"),
  formula =
    y ~
    splines::ns(x1, knots = c(5, 10, 15), Boundary.knots = c(0, 20)) %*%

    Xbeta,
  allow_combine = TRUE,

  data = data
)

summary(fit)
fit$summary.random$Xbeta

On Thu, 23 Sept 2021 at 14:46, Finn Lindgren <finn.l...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hi,
>
> for some reason the plain "Xbeta" use in the predictor doesn't work as intended, but one can access the latent vector directly, which does work.
> One important consideration is also that it's generally unsafe to have completely automated know selections, since if one does that in the predictor expression, one gets different values for estimation and for prediction, so it's much safer to be explicit (can be data dependent, but needs to be controlled to ensure the same values are used in all the calculations).
> See the following example. I'll look into why the direct latent vector access is needed, and also look into other ways of specifying these types of models; they're essentially the same as the 1d-mesh based spde models but with independent priors; those are handled automatically via the main_mapper, and one can make user-defined mapper objects, which could be used to define the "x-to-basis function" mapping for these splines, just as it's done for the B-splines in the 1D mesh models.

James

I am able to add one covariate to the mark, but when I am trying to add more I have the following error:

  Size mismatch for row.kron, (n1, n2) = (1, 0)

Do you know what I am doing wrong?

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] inlabru joint model
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

my first guess would be an issue with the input data object and/or coordinate names; you could try letting inlabru construct the integration by itself, with
  like(..., samplers = boundary, domain = list(coordinates = mesh))
instead of manually supplying ips to see if that makes a difference.
Also, consider the 'include' argument to `like` to tell it which model component are needed by each likelihood; it might be that it's trying to evaluate a model component using data that doesn't allow it to do that (but you're supplying the same data object in both cases, so any issues with that would be due to the integration points)

Otherwise, I may need a complete reproducible code&data example to run here for debugging.
(A small subset of the data would be good; can be simulated, as long as it produces the same error on your system)

Finn

> > > > > > > On Thu, 16 Sept 2021 at 13:54, dan <twitter.is...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > > > > Hi Finn
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > Thank you very much for this quick and thorough response, that helps me a lot. Just to clarify details in you calculation:
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >   theta1 = log(1/sigma^2) = - log(const) + log(kappa) + 2*log(tau)
> > > > > > > >   theta2 = log(rho) = log(kappa)
> > > > > > > > Solving for log(tau) and log(kappa),
> > > > > > > >   log(tau) = -log(const) / 2 + theta1 / 2 + theta2
> > > > > > > >   log(kappa) = theta2,
> > > > > > > > so you need
> > > > > > > >   B.tau = cbind(-log(const) / 2, 1/2, 1)
> > > > > > > >   B.kappa = cbind(0, 0, 1)
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > I got:
> > > > > > > > Solving for log(tau) and log(kappa),
> > > > > > > >   log(tau) = + log(const) / 2 + theta1 / 2 - theta2 /2
> > > > > > > >   log(kappa) = theta2,
> > > > > > > > so you need
> > > > > > > >   B.tau = cbind(+ log(const) / 2, 1/2,  - 1/2)
> > > > > > > >   B.kappa = cbind(0, 0, 1)
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > Do you agree?
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > Assuming that I would like a Gamma prior also for the kappa (alias rho), the call to inla.spde2.matern is then
> > > > > > > > INLA::inla.spde2.matern(
> > > > > > > >   mesh = mesh,
> > > > > > > >   alpha = 1.5,
> > > > > > > >   B.tau = cbind(log(const) / 2, .5, -.5),
> > > > > > > >   B.kappa = cbind(0, 0, 1),
> > > > > > > >   hyper = list(theta1 = list(param = c(a1, a2), prior = "loggamma"),
> > > > > > > >                theta2 = list(param = c(b1, b2), prior = "loggamma"))
> > > > > > > > )?
> > > > > > > > I just ask because there is no hyper argument specified for the inla.spde2.matern and I have learned not to trust the ... argument too much in R.
> > > > > > > > I have to wrap my head around how to get a suitable value for this const and will consider the resources that you have suggested, thanks again.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > Dan
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > finn.l...@gmail.com schrieb am Donnerstag, 16. September 2021 um 12:20:55 UTC+2:
> > > > > > > > > Hi Dan,
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > the sigma-prior is possible; I'm not sure if the "uniform on a finite interval" prior for rho is possible.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > The inla.spde2.matern implements a general family that links a set of theta-parameters to tau and kappa in an spde formulation of the Matern family, (kappa^2-Laplacian)^(alpha/2)(tau x(s)) = W(s) (see the function help text).
> > > > > > > > > The parameter link is user-defined, so allows some flexibility.
> > > > > > > > > Smoothness:
> > > > > > > > >   nu = alpha - dim/2 = 0.5 for alpha=1.5.
> > > > > > > > > Variance:
> > > > > > > > >   sigma^2 = const / kappa^(2*nu) / tau^2
> > > > > > > > > Precision:
> > > > > > > > >   1/sigma^2 = kappa * tau^2 / const
> > > > > > > > > The range controlling parameter rho in your parameterisation is kappa (i.e. rho is proportional to the inverse range), so
> > > > > > > > >   theta1 = log(1/sigma^2) = - log(const) + log(kappa) + 2*log(tau)
> > > > > > > > >   theta2 = log(rho) = log(kappa)
> > > > > > > > > Solving for log(tau) and log(kappa),
> > > > > > > > >   log(tau) = -log(const) / 2 + theta1 / 2 + theta2
> > > > > > > > >   log(kappa) = theta2,
> > > > > > > > > so you need
> > > > > > > > >   B.tau = cbind(-log(const) / 2, 1/2, 1)
> > > > > > > > >   B.kappa = cbind(0, 0, 1)
> > > > > > > > > in order to get theta1 and theta2 to be the log() of 1/sigma^2 and rho.
> > > > > > > > > The constant "const" can be derived from the expression for the variance in Lindgren et al (2011, JRSSB) or Lindgren and Rue 2015 (https://www.jstatsoft.org/article/view/v063i19).
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > You can then set the prior for theta1 to a loggamma(a1,a2) distribution to get your desired prior for 1/sigma^2, via
> > > > > > > > >   hyper=list(theta1=list(...))
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > For theta2, you'd be looking for a prior with density  exp(theta2)/(b2-b1) on the interval (log(b1), log(b2)),
> > > > > > > > > which isn't directly available. I see there's an "expression" prior model that might be able to specify a general density expression, but the finite interval support is bound to cause problems.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > So in summary, yes, it's partly possible, but in particular the rho-prior is a bit problematic, and from a modelling perspective it's probably better to use the pc-prior option via inla.spde2.pcmatern instead.

messages.subject: Correlated Gaussian residuals in INLA
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Is it correct that INLA does not have the option to model correlation between Gaussian residuals?
Instead of using random effects to model the correlation between measurements I would like to model the correlation between measurements using residuals.

Hereby attached is an example model using nlme:
library(nlme)
set.seed(2021)
#Total of N individuals
N<-10
#n=3 correlated measurements per individual
n<-3
data<-data.frame(id=rep(1:N, each=n), y=NA, x=NA)
#setting up data such that the 3 measurements on 1 individual are correlated
for (i in 1:N){
  data$x[(3*(i-1)+1):(3*i)]<-rnorm(1)+rnorm(n, sd=0.1)
}
#Creating response
data$y<-3+2*data$x+rnorm(n*N, sd=0.5)
#fitting using gls with correlated residuals
fm1 <- gls(y ~ 1 + x, data=data,
           correlation = corSymm(form = ~ 1 | id))
#Obtain covariance matrix of correlated residuals
cov2cor(getVarCov(fm1, individual = 1))

The model specification would then look as follows:

Thanks,
Georgy

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Correlated Gaussian residuals in INLA
messages.body_plain:
INLA only support conditional independent data, but for Gaussian
response, you can always just expand the latent field (or linear
predictor) to have define dependent data. sometimes this involve setting
the likelihood to have fixed high precision, like having AR1
depenendency in the observations.

in these cases, you'll end up with a 'fake' linear predictor, for which
a subset of it, is the real one.

there are also generic iid models in dimension up to 10, with general
covariance structure, that can be used for this (see inla.doc("iidkd")
for a new testing version)

Best
H

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] inlabru joint model
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I had to change the mesh construction to a more reasonable size to debug this, but have found the main cause of the problem, which is a bug in how it handles "missing" data, which in this case means model components that are used by only one of the two likelihoods. The intended solution to this problem is to use the include/exclude arguments to like(), an if the models had been purely linear, this would work:

lik1 <- like("cp",

             formula = coordinates ~ .,
             data = data,
             ips = ips,
             include = c("point_field", "Inter_point"),

             )
lik2 <- like("normal",

             formula = size_ha ~ .
             data = data,
             exclude = c("Inter_point"))

Unfortunately, the point_field*scaling term of the second predictor of your model means one has to specify the full expression in the formula, and then the bug is again triggered, in the second INLA iteration.
I'm not yet sure why the bug is triggered in the second step but not the first, so I need to debug some more to find out.

Fortunately, there is a (partly better) alternative, which is to use the INLA "copy" feature to implement the point_field*scaling term.
Use the following model specification:

cmp =
  ~ -1 +

  point_field(coordinates, model = matern) +

  mark_field(coordinates, model = matern) +

  Inter_point(1) + Inter_mark(1) +
  point_field_copy(copy = "point_field", fixed = FALSE) +

  DC+GDP+density+total+rural+agriculture+industry +services +forest

lik1 <- like("cp",

             formula = coordinates ~ .,
             data = data,
             ips = ips,
             include = c("point_field", "Inter_point"),

             )
lik2 <- like("normal",

             formula = size_ha ~ .,
             data = data,
             exclude = c("point_field", "Inter_point"))

I've attached the full working code, including my modified mesh code suggestion that extends the mesh beyond the coastlines and artificial country borders, but sets up the likelihood only on the country bounded domain, just as before.
The mesh has far fewer nodes, making the inference take about 20 seconds, so you could still increase the resolution if you prefer.

Finn

### An example in INLA
set.seed(2021)

### Total of N individuals
N <- 100
### n=3 correlated measurements per individual

n <- 3
data <- data.frame(

    id=rep(1:N, each=n), ### order by individuals!
    x=runif(N*n))

Sigma <- matrix(c(5,-2,1, -2,3,1, 1,1,2), 3)
Sigma
cov2cor(Sigma)
solve(Sigma)

### sampling a covariate setting up data such that the 3 measurements on 1 individual are correlated
errors <- matrix(rnorm(N*n), N) %*% chol(Sigma)
cov(errors)
cor(errors)

data$y <- 3 + 2*data$x + as.vector(t(errors))

library(INLA)

data$i <- as.integer(t(matrix(1:(N*n), N))) ### inla order
res <- inla(y ~ x + f(i, model='iid3d', n=N*n),
            data=data,
            control.family = list(
                hyper = list(
                    prec = list(initial = 15, fixed = TRUE))))
res$summary.fix
res$summary.hy

cbind('TRUE'=c(diag(Sigma), cov2cor(Sigma)[lower.tri(Sigma)]),
      mean=c(1/res$summary.hy$mean[1:n], res$summary.hy$mean[-(1:n)]))

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Correlated Gaussian residuals in INLA
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

This is a different model than the first one. In the first you have correlated residuals, now you have correlated residuals (u_ij) and an additional one (e_ij). This may lead to identifiability issues.

For the first model you asked, the 'iid3d' model in INLA may be considered and so all the three variances are already fitted by this latent model, thus with no likelihood variances needed.

best regards,
Elias

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] inlabru joint model
messages.body_plain:
Hi again,

I got confused earlier; the problem with the predict() call is that you're supplying only a grid of coordinates (masked by the boundary), which is enough to predict the spatial fields, but to predict the given expression across space, you also need to supply the covariate values for all those grid points.
The error message in this case comes when it tries to evaluate the "density" covariate and doesn't find it in the data set, and therefore ends up (due to R features...) finding the _function_ called density, and gets a NULL result. Before it gets to this point, it also tries to evaluate the DC and GDP covariates, but since their names don't appear anywhere at all, they get replaced by 1, for backwards compatibility reasons (I'm looking for a way to make this an error in a safe way, to make it easier to spot this kind of problem).
So the error wasn't quite the same as the one as before, and it was instead a problem with the input data to predict().

Finn
